title: reduce-streaming-token-latency-kernel-scheduling-kv-cache-batching-backpressure
author: Asha Patel
description:
Motivation: Streaming token generation in the runtime has observed 95th/99th percentile token latencies that impact perceived responsiveness for interactive applications. This PR combines several coordinated changes to reduce per-token tail latency: improved kernel scheduling heuristics, adaptive flush cadence for the token streamer, backpressure-aware continuous batching, and KV-cache warmup/lookup optimizations.

Summary of changes: consolidated kernel scheduling policy to prefer low-latency kernels for streaming paths, introduced a fast-path that bypasses heavy kernel selection for short decode horizons, added an adaptive flush cadence controller that emits partially-completed token chunks sooner under low-utilization to reduce head-of-line latency, implemented backpressure signaling from the transport layer to the batching layer (reducing queueing stalls), and optimized KV cache hot-paths to minimize lookup overhead and reduce blocking during cache fills.

Compatibility/risk: All changes are gated behind runtime feature flags and a rolling rollout plan. Default behavior preserves current throughput-mode heuristics; the new latency-optimized mode is enabled for streaming routes by default in this rollout. Kernel heuristic changes include conservative fallbacks to previous selection when performance counters indicate regressions. No API changes.

Testing and validation: microbenchmarks for single-stream latency, end-to-end streaming regression tests, and load tests at 1k/5k concurrent streams were run. Observability additions include per-token latency histograms, batch queue length gauges, and KV cache hit/miss breakdowns for streaming flows. CI includes unit and integration tests exercising the adaptive flush cadence and backpressure signals.

Notes: see related Linear tickets ENG-1428 (streaming latency initiative) and ENG-1489 (KV cache stability).

review_comments: Miguel Torres: Overall LGTM. Two questions: 1) how does the fast-path interact with quantized kernels? 2) can we add a metric for kernel fallback count?

Asha Patel (author): Fast-path respects quantization compatibility and falls back to the existing selection if the quantized kernel is not safe for the requested op/sequence. Added kernel_fallback_count metric in observability commit.
Linh Nguyen: The adaptive flush cadence looks promising. Request: add a unit test that simulates a slow transport to ensure we don't over-emit partial chunks and cause OOM on clients.
Asha Patel (author): Added slow-transport integration test and a guard to limit aggressive flush rate when transport backpressure is high.
Ravi Desai: Performance numbers - can you add a short note in the PR with before/after p50/p95/p99 for a 2k-concurrent-stream load?
Asha Patel (author): Added results to PR description and docs: p50 ~ -3ms, p95 ~ -28ms, p99 ~ -120ms for token emission on a 12B model in our staging cluster under 2k streams.
benchmark_summary: Staging benchmarks against r12 baseline on 12B model, 2000 concurrent streams: token emission p50 improved by 3ms, p95 improved by 28ms, p99 improved by 120ms; overall throughput within 2% of baseline.
release_notes: Reduce streaming token emission tail latency by combining kernel scheduling heuristics, adaptive flush cadence, backpressure-aware batching, and KV cache hot-path optimizations. Rollout behind a feature flag; improvements are non-breaking.
